analysis.one_liner: Directs FDA to set and enforce limits on toxic heavy metals in baby food and juice.
analysis.headline: The Baby Food Safety Act of 2024 was introduced in the Senate with one cosponsor, never received a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to set enforceable limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in foods marketed to babies and toddlers, in fruit and vegetable puree pouches, and in juice. Companies making these foods would have had to test final products at accredited labs, keep records available to inspectors, run environmental monitoring in their plants, and face mandatory recall authority if a contaminated product slipped through. The FDA would also have had to verify companies' own testing and report on imported-food inspections.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with infants and toddlers, who would get federally enforceable limits on the four heavy metals most linked to brain development harm, plus company testing the FDA can check independently. Juice drinkers and parents buying puree pouches are covered too.

how_it_helps.text: The FDA would be required to set public-health limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in infant and toddler food, puree pouches, and juice, with food above those limits treated as adulterated and barred from sale [S2].
Manufacturers would have to test final products for these metals at internationally accredited labs, keep two years of records, and open those records to FDA inspection on request [S2].
The FDA would run its own sampling and testing program to independently verify companies' results, and would gain mandatory recall authority for infant and toddler food found contaminated [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Baby food, puree pouch, and juice makers, who would bear testing, recordkeeping, and plant-monitoring costs, some of which would likely pass to shoppers. The FDA would also need funding to enforce the new limits and run its own testing program.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for testing, lab accreditation, and environmental monitoring would fall on food makers and could raise prices for the packaged baby foods and juice parents buy [S2].
The bill preempts state and local rules on heavy-metal limits, testing, and warning labels in these foods, so no state could set a stricter standard than the federal one [S2].

The schedule is slow: proposed limits for mercury were not required until April 2028, and companies' testing obligations would not start until two years after enactment, leaving children exposed to the status quo in the meantime [S2].
The limits would depend on FDA capacity, and the bill mostly directs the agency to plan and report on imported-food inspections rather than funding a large inspection expansion [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families with young children, the upside is large: heavy metals like lead and arsenic cause measurable developmental harm, and no federal enforceable limits exist for finished baby food. The real costs are compliance expenses for manufacturers and slower timelines than parents might want, and the preemption of stricter state laws is a genuine concession. On balance this is a modest, workable food-safety bill whose main weakness is that it would take years to fully take effect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate health committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 9, 2024, joined by Sen. Tammy Duckworth, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S4][S2].
It attracted one cosponsor in total, and the committee took no further action on it for the remainder of the 118th Congress [S3][S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without ever receiving a committee vote or floor action [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Baby food, puree pouch, and juice manufacturers are better off, since they avoided new testing, contaminant limits, and recall exposure. Parents of young children are no better off than before; there are still no federal limits on heavy metals in finished baby food.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Baby Food Safety Act of 2024 and referred it to the health committee.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup; it received no committee action after its May 2024 referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its only support came from two Democratic senators.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed testing, accredited-lab, environmental monitoring, and recordkeeping costs, and mandatory recall authority for contaminated products — but it also preempts stricter state rules these companies might otherwise face. Without the bill passing, they avoided the costs and keep operating under no enforceable heavy-metal limits for finished baby food.
Limits and testing would have applied to juice and fruit/vegetable puree pouches, an added compliance cost for processors. Consumers of these products would have gained contaminant limits.
The bill required all contaminant testing to be done by internationally accredited labs, creating mandated demand for their services.
